10.2c — Decks: Shuffle, Draw & Traverse

The starter's Shuffle() is EMPTY — check your copy. That emptiness is a gift: the single most exam-famous algorithm of the year, left in the seat where you sit. Today you implement the shuffle, wire the draw, and traverse a hand to render it.

Concept Lab ~10 min

Fisher-Yates, in exam language. The AP pseudocode for a shuffle (know BOTH languages):

AP:                                C#:
FOR i FROM LENGTH(list) TO 2     for (int i = list.Count - 1; i > 0; i--)
    r ← RANDOM(1, i)                 int r = Random.Range(0, i + 1);
    SWAP(list[i], list[r])           (card temp = list[i];
                                     list[i] = list[r];
                                     list[r] = temp;)

Read it as a story: walk the list from the END; at each position, pick a random EARLIER-or-equal position; swap. Every card gets exactly one chance at every slot — that fairness (uniform distribution) is why this is THE textbook shuffle, not a vibe shuffle.

Socratic

The lazy shuffle everyone writes first: repeatedly pick a random card and REMOVE it into a new list. It works — why is it worse than Fisher-Yates (cost per removal: the list shifts every element)? And why does the exam phrase "every possible order is equally likely" make the lazy version suspicious?

Build Lab ~35 min

Step 1 — fill the empty method. In GameManager, implement Shuffle() with the C# above (rename to your list's name — read the starter's Deal() first: it is PARTIALLY implemented, and it shows you the intended list names and the card flow).

Step 2 — the draw, in the starter's voice:

public void Draw()
{
    if (deck.Count == 0)
    {
        // reshuffle the discard pile into the deck — the loop of loops
        return;
    }
    Card topCard = deck[0];
    deck.RemoveAt(0);      // AP: REMOVE(deck, 1)  — index 1 in exam-speak!
    hand.Add(topCard);    // AP: APPEND(hand, topCard)
}

Check the boundary: draw from an EMPTY deck crashes (deck[0] does not exist). The guard clause is the whole difference between a jam build and a jam crash.

Step 3 — traverse to render. A hand is a list; showing it means visiting every element. Two traversal styles, both in the exam:

// index loop — you NEED i for positions:
for (int i = 0; i < hand.Count; i++)
{
    SpawnCardVisual(hand[i], i);
}

// foreach — you only need each card:
foreach (Card c in hand) { Debug.Log(c.cardName); }

Spawn your card prefabs across the screen by index (i sets the x position — the hand literally spreads because of a loop counter). Why does the index loop earn its extra ceremony here? Because position IS the index.

Step 4 — the AP traverse question, answered by your own game: "sum the cost of all cards in hand" — write it in exam pseudocode with your game's real names, then prove the answer with a Debug.Log total.

Bug Hunt: The shuffle bugs

  1. Random.Range(0, i) instead of (0, i + 1). Which card can NEVER move? (The last one! Why — trace i's first value.)
  2. Swapping with a temp VARIABLE FORGOTTEN: list[i] = list[r]; list[r] = list[i]; — what does the deck become, and why does it LOOK shuffled at a glance?
  3. Removing while traversing: a discard-all loop over the hand while removing from it. Which cards get SKIPPED — and why does looping backward fix it exactly (10.2a's warning, now real)?
  4. Draw from an empty deck: what does deck[0] DO when Count is 0? (Try it — read the exception. Then thank the guard clause you wrote.)
Close of Day ~5 min

Tinker: Shuffle science

  1. Test the shuffle like a scientist: shuffle a 3-card deck 60 times, tally the orders. Six possible orders — how close to 10 each? (This is 9.5a thinking: a claim about randomness, CHECKED.)
  2. Commit + push: "10.2c: shuffle + draw + render hand".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Implement Fisher-Yates in C# and match it line by line to AP pseudocode
  • Draw safely with the empty-deck guard
  • Render a hand by index loop (position = index)
  • Explain remove-while-traversing and its backward fix
